brief.summary: Swarm Defense builds small drones, and the software that lets one operator fly several of them, in Auburn Hills, Michigan. Products include the Kiwi, a quadcopter ordered in a one-way attack configuration, and target drones for counter-drone training. It says it grew out of Firefly Drone Shows, a light-show drone maker.
brief.thesis: Swarm Defense announced a minimum $25 million Department of War order for 4,000 Kiwi attack drones. The only equity on record is $1,435,000. The company says its swarm control software was developed over eight years of drone light shows.
brief.stage: A Form D filed 17 April 2026 reports $1,435,000 of equity sold to 10 investors (one non-accredited) and names none. FPDS shows $1,174,176 obligated across three awards. The company won no delivery order after Gauntlet I, placed fifth in Gauntlet II deep strike, and announced the minimum $25 million, 4,000-drone prototype order on 22 September 2026. It was not in FPDS on 2 October 2026.

brief.summary: Deployable Energy Limited is a Houston company developing the Unity Nuclear Battery, a 1 MWe helium-cooled, water-moderated microreactor using 4.95% enriched uranium dioxide fuel. The company says units will be factory built and refuelled on a five-year cycle. A demonstration reactor completed a zero-power criticality test at Idaho National Laboratory on 30 June 2026.
brief.thesis: It reached criticality in roughly 150 days using 4.95% enriched fuel rather than HALEU. Its stated markets (defense, maritime, remote industry, data centers) and a Houston facility it says is intended for high-volume production fit energy, defense and manufacturing.
brief.stage: Solaris's 10-Q filed 6 August 2026 says it invested $5.0 million in June 2026 in a SAFE with a $150.0 million post-money cap. Deployable said on 17 August 2026 that Hornbeck Offshore also invested, amount not given. EDGAR shows no Form D. No source opened names other investors, a total raised or a priced round. The company told the NRC it plans a construction permit application by 1 December 2026.

USAspending lists eight contracts starting between January 2022 and September 2025 totalling $5,806,113.94, plus three NASA grants totalling $8,763,972. The SAM record (mirrored) gives a start date of 5 November 2019. The FCC granted three special temporary authorities for radar operation at 55 to 75 kft from 8 to 30 September 2026.

unverified: A search summary attributes an Andreessen Horowitz seed and Series A to Aloft Sensing. No page opened supports it, and it most likely refers to a different Aloft.
NASA says the instrument was validated aboard an airship at 65,000 feet and on small stratospheric balloons, but gives no dates, platform names or results. Not independently confirmed.

robocurve.description: Robocurve builds open-source tools and independent benchmarks to measure how well robots can do real-world jobs. Instead of relying on unverified demo videos from frontier labs, we score their models on reproducible benchmarks that anyone can trust. Today there are no well-run, standardized robotics benchmarks. Labs evaluate in-house, and no independent group has stepped in to run continuous benchmarking as a service. The result is that no one actually knows how good anyone else is, or where the real frontier sits. Good benchmarks require operating and maintaining physical hardware and real-world setups. Simulation only goes so far, since models that look strong in sim can show large performance gaps once deployed in the real world. Building real-world benchmarks means coordinating job-domain experts, evals engineering, and hands-on robotics all at once. Frontier labs are targeting general-purpose robotics by 2028, yet the field of robotics evals barely exists. Whoever builds the trusted measure of robot capability becomes the reference everyone relies on. We combine backgrounds in AI evals and robotics to build and grow this field as fast as possible. We already shipped v1 of our open-source framework, Inspect Robots, and ran our first pilot scoring a frontier model on a real robot.

brief.thesis: FANCO pairs energy with manufacturing: a 240 MWe reactor designed for factory fabrication, a proposed fuel plant, and a plan announced with the State of Indiana (reported at more than $4 billion) for manufacturing facilities and an energy park.
brief.stage: Five Form Ds report $13,687,050 sold: $1,250,000 of $2,500,000 in equity (filed 30 June 2025), $20,000 of $5,000,000 in SAFEs (29 August 2025), $10,000,000 from one investor (15 December 2025), $1,417,050 from four (22 December 2025), and $1,000,000 of $25,000,000 in equity and debt from one investor (18 September 2026). The filings name no investors. No round announcement was found. The company targets power from EAGL-1 by 2033.

Is there a signed customer or site for the Bridge Power phase, and why is the CTO announced in April 2026 not on the team page?

brief.summary: Rosota is a Seoul startup, described by press and its own site as a spin-off of the MediSC lab at Seoul National University Hospital. Press reports say it is developing SurgiLogger, a device that attaches to existing laparoscopic instruments and records motion, force and video, to train a surgical robotics foundation model.
brief.thesis: The fit is robotics, not defense, energy or manufacturing. A preprint under review reports a policy trained on 849 logger-recorded demonstrations completing an appendectomy in three of four live rabbits, with the surgeon selecting each surgical phase.
brief.stage: Seed stage. On 2 July 2026 Korean press reported a KRW 1.5 billion seed round led by FuturePlay with Schmidt and ZDVC (WowTale's English edition gives $965K). No valuation or terms were reported. Press later reported selection for a Seoul Business Agency Silicon Valley accelerator program with 500 Global (4 August 2026) and for the TIPS R&D general track (2 October 2026, amount not stated).

questions: Who owns the logger, the data pipeline and the policy work, Rosota or SNU Hospital? All ten Rosota-affiliated preprint authors also list a hospital or university affiliation.
Money Today says founded May 2026, the CEO's page says CEO since January 2025. When was the company incorporated, and who is full time today?
Has the device been used in human surgery, and under what approvals? The logger preprint says operating-room validation remains future work.
Is the business an AI-native surgical robot or a foundation model supplied to other companies? What stays proprietary given both appendectomy training corpora are publicly released?
risks: Evidence is early and narrow. The in-vivo result is one rollout in each of four rabbits on a single day (three completed). All six preprints are not yet accepted.
The only reported funding is the KRW 1.5 billion seed and a TIPS grant (size undisclosed). The stated goal is a surgical robot. No source read gives a regulatory plan.
Closely tied to the hospital lab. The site lists the CEO as still enrolled in medical school. No source read states how IP, data rights or staff time are split.
unverified: The founding date is not confirmed. Money Today says May 2026, the CEO's page lists his role from January 2025. No registry record or company statement was found.
No source gives the co-founders' titles or current roles, or states whether co-founder Lee Dong-ho is the preprint author Dongho Yee.
The CEO's personal page says Rosota was selected for the KISED Deep-Tech Startup Package program. This is self-reported and not confirmed elsewhere.

brief.summary: Chariot Defense builds Amphora, a family of transportable battery power systems for military units. The systems take energy from tactical generators, vehicles, wall power or solar, store it, and distribute it under software control. The Form D, USAspending and the job board give San Bruno as its location.
brief.thesis: Drones, counter-UAS, electronic warfare and directed energy all draw on the same tactical power supply. Chariot has a company-announced $7.6 million DIU contract to deliver to Army brigades, but the Series A is already done, led by Andreessen Horowitz.
brief.stage: Series A. A Form D filed 25 February 2026 shows $33,160,085 sold of $34,600,000 to 16 investors. The same-day release calls it a $34 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz, total funding $41 million after an $8 million seed in July 2025. USAspending shows $74,900 obligated. The company announced a $7.6 million DIU contract on 24 August 2026, then gave $7.4 million. No source gives a valuation.

Which Army office would buy at scale after PRISM, and what depends on the Army xTech Adaptive Strike final exercise reportedly scheduled for October to November 2026?
What is revenue to date, and how does it split between the Army, DIU and the unnamed commercial customers the Series A release mentions?
What are unit price, gross margin and monthly output for Amphora 24 and Amphora 400, and who besides Adam Warmoth leads engineering and manufacturing?
risks: The round is recent and crowded. Andreessen Horowitz led the $34 million Series A in February 2026 with nine other named funds participating. No source gives a valuation.
Government money on record is small against $41 million raised. USAspending shows $74,900 obligated. The DIU contract rests on company releases, and no source names a program of record.
Performance figures are company-reported and not consistent. The DIU release says up to 60 percent fuel reduction, the company site says up to 45 percent.
unverified: Tectonic Defense gives Amphora 400 capacity as 315 kWh, while the company site lists 15 kWh. The discrepancy is not resolved.
Tectonic Defense reports Warmoth saying Amphora was tested by the 101st Airborne and Marine Corps teams and is deployed outside the US. No government source was found.
Military and Aerospace Electronics reports that Chariot is a finalist in the Army's xTech Adaptive Strike competition. This is not confirmed against the Army's competition page.

questions: What has the prototype measured since June 2024 (power curve, annual energy per square metre against a conventional rotor), and has any third party verified it?
The abstracts of the two acquired US patents do not mention a cowling. Which claims cover the cowling design, and what has Aerovec filed in its own name?
The amended Form C says predecessor Kean Wind Turbines ceased operations in 2019 following fundraising restrictions linked to a New York Attorney General investigation. What did it conclude?
Cash was $14,341.64 at 31 March 2026 and the Air Force performance period ended 30 September 2026. What funds the company now, and is there a follow-on proposal?
risks: Very thin capital. Filings show $507,000 of seed preferred and $115,790.56 from Reg CF. Cash was $14,341.64 at 31 March 2026, and the amended Form C flags going concern doubt.
Technology unproven in public. The amended Form C says only a prototype has been manufactured. No test data, certification or paid pilot appears in the filings or on the website.
The IP is acquired and ageing. Both US patents were assigned by Kean Wind Turbines Inc., claim a June 2009 priority and expire in 2030 and 2032 per Google Patents.
unverified: The company claims letters of support from a US Air Force innovation officer and United Rentals (which it calls not final or binding). No letter was seen.
The SBIR phase and topic of the Air Force order are not confirmed from a primary source. HigherGov, an aggregator, lists SBIR Phase I. USAspending states no phase.
The New York Attorney General investigation into Kean Wind Turbines is known only from one sentence in the amended Form C. No Attorney General record was opened.

questions: The company's LinkedIn page names three Ohio departments flying the Trio Scout. How many units have shipped in total, and what revenue has that produced?

Who are the 39 investors behind the $3,992,500, what are the SAFE caps and note terms, and why did the August 2026 amendment add debt and convertible notes?

The financing is small: $3,992,500 over about 32 months from 39 investors on SAFEs and notes. The filings name no investors and none checks the equity box.
unverified: The company's LinkedIn page says three Ohio departments flew missions of 64, 75 and 80 minutes. No department statement or news report confirming these was found.
A search snippet said its systems are already deployed with the US Army. The Army page shows only participation in a prize competition.

brief.summary: Hebbian Robotics (San Francisco, per the YC directory) builds software that checks the quality of robot and egocentric video data before it is used to train models. Its main product is HFlow, an Apache-2.0 SDK (pre-v1). It also offers hosted checks and models in preview, and Pareto, a dataset curation tool in public beta.
brief.thesis: Hebbian targets a step before training, for both vendors who collect robot data and teams who train on it. It is a tooling bet on robot learning rather than on one robot. Evidence so far is open source activity only.
brief.stage: Formation stage. YC lists the company in its Summer 2026 batch. A founder's LinkedIn post of 14 September 2026 refers to YC Demo Day as already held. questions: No customer is named on any page read. How many customers are paying, are they data vendors or robotics teams, and what is the revenue?
HFlow is Apache-2.0 and runs in the customer's own environment. What is sold: hosted model calls at $1.16 per video-hour, managed workspaces, or custom checks per customer?
The homepage compares hbr-preview with two general models on throughput and cost only. What is its measured accuracy, on what test set, and what was it trained on?
The 2 July 2026 YC announcement said the goal was human-like robots for infrastructure field work. Is building robots still the plan? What has been raised beyond YC?
risks: No proven business model. The SDK is free. Founders wrote on 31 August 2026 that they are considering managed workspaces and enterprise support. No customer or revenue figure is public.
Robotics teams may build this themselves. A Launch HN commenter said many robotics teams prefer in-house tools. Kingston Kuan replied that the founders have had the same experience.
Direction has moved several times in 2026: cleaning robot prototype, robots for data centers, human-like field robots, curation, quality APIs, the HFlow SDK, hosted models. Team of 2, per YC.
unverified: An archived homepage of 24 August 2026 claimed unnamed angels from Oracle, Google DeepMind and OpenAI. The current homepage no longer does. No independent confirmation, no amounts.
Founder Factor's LinkedIn post congratulates listed companies on their "successful raises" but gives no amount, instrument or date for Hebbian. No round announcement by the company was found.
Brandon Ong's claims (LionsBot being Series B, Gigit AI backed by Sequoia India, topping the SEA-HELM benchmark) appear on his YC profile and launch post, not independently confirmed.

brief.summary: Salem Robotics sells autonomy software that lets existing mobile robots (Boston Dynamics Spot is one, a co-founder says) run surveys and inspections in hazardous facilities. It started with radiological surveys at nuclear sites and says it is also working on oil, gas and hazardous chemical facilities. The Form D gives an Austin, Texas address.
brief.thesis: Nuclear sites must run routine radiation surveys and largely do them by hand. Salem sells software for robots sites may already own, touching robotics and energy without building hardware. Both founders co-authored a February 2024 paper on robot radiation surveys.
brief.stage: A Form D filed on 8 September 2026 reports $1,819,500 sold of a $5,100,000 SAFE offering to 5 unnamed investors, first sale 13 May 2026. Y Combinator lists the company in its Summer 2026 batch. Non Sibi Ventures is the only other investor confirmed by its own pages (a $25,000 Rice prize investment in April 2026, and it says it backed the company beyond that, no amount given).

questions: Which facilities have signed a paid validation, at what price, and has any converted into an ongoing deployment? The Launch HN post names no customer.
Who are the 5 SAFE investors and what are the caps? How much did Non Sibi invest beyond the $25,000 Rice prize, and is Goose Capital an investor?
Incorporated in 2024 per the Form D, first SAFE sale 13 May 2026. What happened in between, and do UT Austin or Los Alamos hold any rights?

The launch post claims theoretical safety guarantees. What exactly is guaranteed, and has any site radiation protection program or regulator accepted robot-generated survey records as compliance records?
risks: No source shows a signed customer, a paid validation or a deployment. The company's 4 August 2026 launch post speaks of "active contract-scoping conversations" in nuclear and oil and gas.
The product is a software layer on other companies' robots. A robot maker could move into this layer. The founders' Launch HN post asks where the line should sit.
Public records do not line up. Y Combinator says founded 2026 in San Francisco with a team of 2. The Form D says incorporated 2024 with an Austin address.
unverified: The company site shows a Goose Capital logo. No Goose Capital page found confirms an investment, and Rice's 2026 results list its prizes going to other companies.
Non Sibi Ventures says both founders hold top-secret clearances, not confirmed by any primary source.
The launch post says the manipulation framework rests on founder research published in IEEE journals and conferences. Those papers were not located.

nori.description: We manufacture Nori: A sub-$2000 bimanual mobile manipulator that can clean rooms, restock shelves, and fold clothes. Nori can handle basic tasks out of the box, and its software lets anyone teach Nori to automate work specific to their home or business. Nori aims to solve the robotics data bottleneck. By deploying affordable robots to customers around the world, we can gather the diverse data required to train the next generation of generalist robotic policies. Every user of Nori makes Nori smarter. Since launching 6 weeks ago we have already deployed our first robot and have over $440k+ in sales. We can bring general-purpose robotics to homes and businesses that could never afford it before. There are 132.7 million households and 8.4 million employer business locations in the U.S. At $1,688 per robot, selling just one Nori to 0.5% of them represents a $1.2B market opportunity in the U.S. alone.

facts.bio: Antonio is the founder of Nori Robotics. He studied Computer Science and Architecture at Columbia, where he held research fellowships with the Laidlaw Scholars Program, the Data Science Institute, and the Graphics & UI Lab. His research focused on teaching robots new tasks through VR demonstrations. He also holds a national patent for a computer-vision system, and previously co-founded Truely, which grew to 2,000+ users and 1.5M+ impressions.

super-powers-mobility-spm.description: We started off building the highest performance, 470 volt electric off-road vehicles but we realized our ultra power dense battery packs are useful for mobile and stationary energy storage and power export, for military and consumer use cases. We develop battery packs, power electronics, and traction powertrain systems for vehicles. For the majority of 2026 we were marketing our electric off-road vehicles, but we pivoted to selling our high performance battery packs and power export capabilities in the month of September. We went from having $769,000 in consumer pre-orders (possibly low conversion rate to sales) to $421,815 in realized revenue in 1 month, with a $792,000 qualified pipeline. Our tech is so compelling because the safety and layout of high voltage battery packs has only been mastered by large, well funded OEM companies who have brought it in-house. That means all other companies without the in-house expertise rely on battery companies to develop packs, and power electronics companies to develop power export capabilities. SPM has both of those capabilities in-house so we can ensure a fast turnaround and much more reliable product. One of the biggest priorities of the department of war is energy dominance. We're seeing it constantly in new solicitations. Our strategy is superior - become a prime, but simultaneously service primes because most of then don't actually have the battery and power electronics expertise we have. Founded by Jon Powers - Ex-Tesla Sr. Mechanical Integration Engineer leading Cybertruck vehicle integration.

facts.bio: Founder/CEO at Super Powers Mobility (YC F26). Previously Senior Mechanical Design Engineer at Tesla, leading Cybertruck architecture integration including drive units, structures, exterior surfaces, occupant seating, low and high voltage distribution routing, and safety systems. Earlier lead brake system on electric vehicle development at Workhorse and powersports design at Honda R&D. MS & BS in Mechanical Engineering, MBA from Pitt. Also was a pro off-road racer during college.

hundred.description: Hundred is an automated inspection system for the components that make up consumer devices like phones, smartwatches, and laptops. Hundred helps factories cut waste and prevent line-down issues by catching sub-100µm cosmetic defects before parts reach the assembly line. In the consumer electronics industry, designs change so fast that traditional machine vision can't keep up, forcing factories to rely on manual inspection, literally people checking parts under microscopes to sort out bad parts. Human inspectors miss roughly 15% of defects, and a single bad part can turn a finished device into scrap. Hundred is replacing manual inspection with an imaging rig that scans an entire shipping tray of parts at once. The Hundred rig blocks ambient light and uses varied controlled lighting configurations to detect defects smaller than 100µm on a range of materials. The controlled environment means Hundred only needs to scan a single good part before it can find defects, categorize them, and assess their severity accurately. Defects cost U.S. discrete manufacturers $45 billion a year, a problem Hundred's CEO, Erica, saw firsthand as a mechanical engineer designing devices at Meta, Google, and Magic Leap. She met Imani, Hundred's CPO, at Columbia University's admitted-students day in 2017 and Imani went on to spend five years at Twitch building software that handles billions of requests a day. Erica later met Iris, Hundred's CTO, in the Bay Area. Iris worked as a quant at Citadel before pivoting to study at Imperial College London where she researched machine learning on 3D meshes and other structured data. Together, they're building Hundred because manual inspection shouldn't still exist in 2026.

rodeo-robotics.description: Rodeo builds a robotic technician that automates maintenance so fleets can get vehicles back on the road sooner. Initial deployments focus on oil changes at centralized depots, where routine maintenance competes for scarce technician time. Cofounders Michael Hazard and Colby Duke met at Applied Intuition, where they worked with OEMs like Toyota and General Motors to bring software and autonomy to vehicles. They saw firsthand how much manual work it takes to keep vehicle fleets running, and learned how to make autonomy reliable through structured testing, real-world data, and human intervention. They’re now applying their experience to the roughly $600B annual US vehicle maintenance market. The average US vehicle is older than ever, driving up maintenance demand at a time when shops already struggle to hire and retain technicians. That gap leaves fleets facing costly downtime and preventable breakdowns. Despite this need, vehicle maintenance has resisted traditional automation. Service information is fragmented and unreliable, and vehicle hardware varies significantly between makes and models. Rodeo builds on advances in robotic foundation models to learn maintenance skills that transfer across vehicles. Rodeo pairs robots with human technicians who ensure each job is completed correctly, handling work the robots can’t yet perform autonomously. These deployments generate training data for Rodeo’s models through both teleoperation and hand tools augmented to record how technicians work. This lets Rodeo earn revenue while collecting the data needed to automate more of each job and improve margins.

facts.bio: Building robots for vehicle maintenance. Four years at Applied Intuition bringing software and autonomy to vehicles. Google APM. Stanford CS.
Building robots for vehicle maintenance. Previously the tech lead of Applied Intuition's neural simulation team.
